rewrites.5EF291F2: The marker was the model's assumption, not a measured cap. At the international routes' 76.0% load factor, 1.8 million inbound seats would carry about 1.37 million arrivals, fewer than the 1.57 million ACSA recorded in FY25/26. The model gives no seat table, load factors or frequencies behind the figure (Appendix A2). What binds in practice is the runway at peak hours in summer, at about 30 movements an hour. No source yet gives peak-hour or seasonal slot headroom.[^134]
rewrites.3DBD9F9E: The question is what the target requires. At a load factor of 80%, 2.5 million arrivals imply about 3.1 million inbound seats a year. The year to November 2025 held about 1.9 million each way, so the target needs about 1.2 million more, roughly two thirds more than today. The base case of 2.18 million arrivals implies about 2.7 million seats, some 0.8 million more. These are orders of magnitude, because arrivals and passengers are counted on different bases. The model owner should confirm them.[^135]
rewrites.5046D10B: The target rests on eight requirements; conversion and longer stays need no new seat.
rewrites.236415A3: The Infrastructure Report treats supply as three layers. The weakest layer limits how a destination performs (Table 2.14). Strong attractions cannot make up for missing services or access: poor access keeps visitors away and weak services shorten their stay and cut their spend. Services and infrastructure without attractions, in turn, draw too little demand.[^138]
rewrites.109B75CB: The layers nest and a weak one fails in its own way (Figure 2.15).
rewrites.1A03D23D: Each layer answers a different question for the visitor and every mapped asset is sorted into one of them.
rewrites.25935A40: Each region is scored from 1 to 5 on attractiveness (40%), readiness and capacity (30%) and accessibility (30%). The scores compare regions without measuring absolute quality. Appendix A4 sets out the method and its limits. One limit bears on every count below: the supply dataset includes generated placeholder records and holds no geography below district level, so the asset total is provisional.[^139]
rewrites.54DDDD3F: Cape Town has won more routes than its peers (section 2.2). Ten airlines fly to Cape Town International from Africa, nine from Europe, three from North and South America, two from the Middle East and one, Singapore Airlines, from Asia. Twenty-nine international routes serve the airport in 2026. Cape Town's share of South Africa's international capacity rose from 10% in 2010 to 25%.[^140]
rewrites.1B492C39: Cape Town's seven largest international markets are all hub airports and their seats have grown since 2019 (above). Western Europe holds 38% of international capacity, the Middle East 23%, Southern Africa 17%, Eastern Africa 14% and North America 6%. Most hub passengers connect: Emirates' connecting share is above 80% a year and Qatar Airways' is nine in ten.[^144]
rewrites.63B4A348: Yet no seat flies direct to Asia: the network has no direct capacity to any Asian market. Thirteen of the 27 routes in the load table serve African or Indian Ocean points and none serves Asia. A direct Asian route is a long-term prize. The near-term seats sit with the hub carriers. The hub routes are not full. Dubai ran at 72.3%, Addis Ababa at 71.9% and Doha at 65.2% in the year to November 2025. On those routes marketing can still fill seats, which it cannot do on the eleven full ones.[^146]
rewrites.5D8B8EDC: In 2026 the hub model showed its risk. About one third of passengers to or from Asia-Pacific used Middle East hubs in 2025, on IATA's May 2026 count. In September 2026 Middle East carriers' international demand fell 7.5%, while African carriers' rose 8.0%. Emirates had 91% of its previous network operating at 30 September and its April to September passengers fell 22%. Qatar Airways had suspended four Saudi destinations, not its hub. ACSA's warning of 1 March 2026 included Cape Town. Hubs in one conflict region share risk, so spreading work across Dubai and Doha alone gives false comfort.
rewrites.726BA2A7: Alternatives are growing. British Airways added Cape Town capacity in March 2026, ahead of the larger winter schedule. Emirates launched its third daily service on 1 July 2026. Emirates also widened its codeshare with South African Airways in August, though a codeshare through Dubai is not an independent routing. Wesgro's 2024/25 record was one additional airline, four international routes and ten expansions.
rewrites.5E7D94C6: At the peak, the runway paces growth. Cape Town International has one main runway and no parallel taxiway, which caps movements at about 30 an hour. The cap binds in the morning and evening flight banks and from November to March, not off-peak. Relocating the runway lifts it to 45 movements an hour, a 50% rise. On the planning timeline the runway completes around 2033, with terminal relief from about 2032. ACSA's latest schedule builds the realigned runway between December 2026 and December 2029, subject to contract award. ACSA's own stakeholder presentation of May 2025 gave completion in 2031. This report assumes about 2033 and treats the earlier dates as upside.[^149]
rewrites.5551EE77: Two of the airport's seven components are full and four are under strain (Table 2.15). The runway and the domestic arrivals hall, the first thing a visitor connecting through Johannesburg or Durban meets, have reached their limits. The site is boxed in between the runway and the roads, so the fix has to move the runway itself. ACSA's programme of about R11.3 billion targets every problem area. The risk is timing, not scope. The runway still needs regulatory sign-off and terminals take five to seven years to build, so each peak before relief runs tighter than the last.[^150]
rewrites.410EF13F: The terminals and aircraft stands sit between the runway and the roads. Six of the seven components are full or under strain (Figure 2.18).
rewrites.6650451E: Two of the seven components are full and four are under strain; fixes are itemised and dated for four of those six.
rewrites.210ED903: ACSA's February 2026 programme prices the works. The realigned runway, at about R6.39 billion, is 3,500 m by 60 m, rotated 11.5 degrees and Code F capable, with contractor appointment planned for December 2026. Domestic arrivals works come to R2.39 billion, a domestic departures expansion from April 2027 to R500 million and international terminal development to R863 million. This is an investment programme, not a construction possession and slot timetable. Its items come to about R10.1 billion, against the R11.3 billion overhaul in the Infrastructure Report. The two are not reconciled.
rewrites.6D181699: George is full today and its fix is small, funded and near. The airport handled 911,000 two-way passengers in 2025, above the roughly 900,000 its terminal was built for. A R310 million terminal expansion doubles capacity to about 2 million passengers a year by 2028 or 2029, with construction from October 2026. George is a domestic airport, so international visitors connect through another gateway. Reliability is the open risk: fog and wind divert flights and a lapse in landing-system approvals cancelled more than ten flights in one day in January 2025.[^151]
rewrites.547B02F6: Cape Winelands Airport stays a scenario, not committed capacity. It is a private development at the old Fisantekraal airfield, some 30 km north of the city, with a first phase of about R8 billion. Its 3.5 km runway could take long-haul aircraft, its terminal is designed for 5.2 million passengers a year and it targets first passengers in 2028. Environmental appeals were dismissed in May 2026, but financial close, aviation licensing and airline commitments are not yet evidenced. Capacity and certainty pull apart: the certain fix comes last and the earliest large option is the least certain.[^152]
rewrites.3F1FC01F: The two smaller airfields do not change the picture to 2035. Plettenberg Bay has holiday demand but a 1,220m unlit runway (too short for larger regional aircraft) and one seasonal route to Johannesburg. Beaufort West has a lit 1,483m runway, a control tower and jet fuel, but no scheduled flights and too few travellers to fill them. The Infrastructure Report advises a watching brief on the first and no further work on the second.[^153]
rewrites.12C1566F: Cruise visits fell back in 2025/26 with no change in berth capacity. The province hosted 70, 67 and 79 vessels in the 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 seasons, carrying 144,125, 109,884 and 127,178 passengers. Wesgro counts 64 cruise liner visits, 106,240 passengers and 37,200 crew for 2025/26. The full study for that season, with unique and international passengers, is not in hand. That season added R1.35 billion to provincial GDP-R from R1.47 billion of spending and supported 1,701 full-time equivalent jobs in the province. The season before, Wesgro counted 79 cruise liner visits and 83 vessel calls; cruise added R1.79 billion to GDP-R after displacement, with 1,234 direct and 2,345 total jobs.[^154]
rewrites.6BA7AA83: Berth space is not the limit. The single equipped berth can take 150 or more calls a season. Its limits are a 300m ship length, the South-Easter wind and the lack of shore power. The demand base is volatile. International passengers rose from 55,495 in 2022/23 to 100,255 in 2024/25, about 81% more; the 2025/26 split is not in hand. Reroutes made 20 of the 67 calls in 2023/24. Red Sea diversions reverse when shipping normalises. The Diagnostic also rates the Port of Cape Town a binding constraint, with congestion and equipment failures affecting export and cruise reliability. Growth is set by the regional circuit that brings a ship for a season and by shore capacity on call days.[^155]
rewrites.7123CABC: Ships come for the circuit, not for one port. A line deploys a ship for a season when a full itinerary works. Wesgro's prospectus sells Cape Town as the homeport for two. The east coast itinerary calls at Mossel Bay and Hermanus, then at Gqeberha, East London, Durban and Richards Bay. It runs on to Mozambique, the East African coast and the Indian Ocean islands. The west coast itinerary runs through Saldanha Bay and Port Nolloth to Namibia, Angola and St Helena. The province holds one equipped port in that circuit. Mossel Bay handled 21 calls and about 13,000 passengers and opened a R22 million passenger facility in November 2025, yet ships anchor and tender there and only small and mid-sized ships call. Saldanha Bay has had 3 trial calls into an ore terminal, with no cruise berth or passenger facility. Calls rise when the circuit works, not when Cape Town markets harder. Mossel Bay's own count differs: calls rose from four before COVID-19 to 27 a season. The Cruise Economic Contribution Study counts 21 passenger-day visits there in 2024/25, with 31,146 passengers and R46.3 million of spending. For 2025/26 Wesgro counts 13 cruise liner visits across Mossel Bay, Hermanus and Saldanha Bay together, with just over 7,150 passengers and R11.2 million of spending. The counts follow different definitions and are not reconciled.[^156]
rewrites.50BE08EB: Port capital is not going to cruise. Saldanha's R4 billion upgrade serves iron ore and Cape Town's port project is a container expansion, which leaves the Mossel Bay facility as the only cruise capital in the pipeline. The Infrastructure Report therefore reads cruise growth as a task of demand and product, not of capital works. Mossel Bay reports that its early excursion information was too limited and that a broader, professionally packaged offer drew more value from each call.[^157]
rewrites.28E2DD57: Shore capacity binds on call days. A call lands its passengers in the same few hours. The prospectus sells them the Cape Town Big 6, among them Table Mountain, Cape Point, Robben Island and the V&A Waterfront. Those are the sites the next subsection finds full in season. The terminal has queue space for about ten coaches. When two liners docked on one day in March 2025 with just over 5,000 passengers, the City warned the public to expect congestion around the Waterfront. The cruise season falls in the southern summer, so more peak calls compound peak pressure.[^158]
rewrites.7442D0E7: The province's best-known sites run at capacity in summer. The Table Mountain Aerial Cableway reports peak queues of up to three hours up and two down. It also reports high winds that close it for a large part of the year. It adds that road congestion can turn a visit into a full day and that tourists do not use the MyCiTi service. Environmental restrictions and public sensitivity leave little scope for permanent building on the summit. Chapman's Peak suffers disruptions, the December and January peak overwhelms transport and accommodation capacity and Boulders is already near carrying capacity.[^160]
rewrites.6DBE220C: Three flagships are each seen by more than half of international tourists and visits to four of them rose by more than 40% in 2023.
rewrites.3FC8E9D9: Counts for 2025 show the same pressure. The City's fourth-quarter figures record 374,808 visits to the Cableway, 337,044 to Cape Point, 202,047 to Kirstenbosch and 108,225 to Robben Island. Table Mountain National Park recorded 1,708,289 entries from April to October 2025. Visits are neither distinct tourists nor safe capacities. From 1 November 2026 SANParks charges South African adults R57 and international adults R282 at Boulders and international adults R592 at Cape Point. Stony Point's R45 entry and opening hours establish neither spare ecological capacity nor readiness for coaches.
rewrites.71A468A2: The Cape Metro holds 72.5% of provincial GDPR and 40% of the province's tourism assets; accessibility falls with each step away from it.
rewrites.0DB978A9: Overall readiness halves between the Metro and the periphery. The Cape Metro rates 4.5 out of 5, the Cape Winelands and the Garden Route 3.4, the Overberg 2.7, the West Coast 2.5 and the Central Karoo 1.9. Accessibility falls fastest (Table 2.17). The six profiles below show what lies behind each rating.[^167]
rewrites.572CDEEF: The Metro carries the volume. About 11.1 million two-way passengers used Cape Town International in 2025, 3.3 million of them international. Both streams grew 7% on the year. Its asset base is the deepest in the province, with 6,563 accommodation records, 6,532 eateries and 5,544 attractions. The maps show that depth packed into a few corridors. Heritage, cruise, retail and cultural attractions crowd into one gateway precinct, which absorbs demand and also bottlenecks it. Natural tourism rests on the mountain and peninsula spine. Premium beds line the Atlantic Seaboard and dining runs from the Waterfront to Camps Bay. Township attractions, food and accommodation sit outside those circuits. Industrial belts convert none of their nearby attractions into tourism.[^168]
rewrites.531CD032: The Garden Route is the province's second tourism region and its strongest multi-day product. Accommodation is its largest asset category (with 4,996 records) and 65.5% of its visitors stay overnight. Attractions, beds and restaurants run along the N2 in separate nodes: Knysna's lagoon and guesthouses, the coast, villas and resorts of Plettenberg Bay and the adventure hub and forest lodging at Tsitsikamma. Mossel Bay and Wilderness form secondary clusters. Inland of the N2 the district is largely inactive for tourism, seasonal swings leave occupancy uneven and indoor entertainment and meeting facilities are thin.[^170]
rewrites.71A91173: The N2 is the district's sole transport spine. George Airport adds access and the Outeniqua Choo Tjoe line has heritage potential, but passenger rail is limited and no shuttle links the towns. The Department of Mobility cites the George Integrated Public Transport Network as evidence that affordable, reliable local transport can support tourism in secondary destinations. The pipeline lifts the air bottleneck through the George terminal and a R9.4 million landing-system upgrade. It leaves no international carrier, a deep winter trough and unfunded gaps in transport between nodes and in product at Mossel Bay and George. FEDHASA points to the Discover Garden Route partnership as a platform for a regional proposition. Mossel Bay reports inconsistent restaurant quality and service. It is expanding roads as demand grows.[^171]
rewrites.1BDC0829: The Cape Winelands is the province's premium food and wine district and the nearest dispersal region to Cape Town. About 1.5 million visitors a year go to its participating attractions, on Wesgro's 2025 estimate. Visitor numbers fell while bed-nights rose by 20.2% for domestic and 37.5% for international visitors, over a period the source does not state. Wine estates dominate its 2,298 attraction records. The Stellenbosch, Franschhoek and Paarl corridor holds most of the attractions, beds and restaurants. Mid-market accommodation is effectively absent outside Stellenbosch. A product mix skewed to luxury excludes mid-market and family segments. Supply also tightens without warning in harvest, in wedding weeks and in the winter off-season.[^172]
rewrites.5F7255C3: The West Coast offers nature, fishing villages and spring flowers within reach of Cape Town, on a thin service base. About 450,000 visitors a year go to its participating attractions, on a count with no stated year. Its tourism economy rests on the Langebaan, Saldanha and Paternoster corridor. Self-catering and guesthouses dominate its 2,294 accommodation records. Hotels, eco-lodges and graded inland stock are scarce. Demand peaks in the August to September flower season and operators close out of season. The West Coast District Municipality reports that proximity to Cape Town drives overflow and day trips (a major part of its recent growth) and that the flower season brings international visitors.[^174]
rewrites.7E0B1CEE: Access is by road alone. The R27 and N7 carry almost all visitors, services thin out beyond Langebaan, Vredenburg and Saldanha and the northern municipalities have no passenger rail. Transport, enabling structure and activity attractions are its lowest category scores, at 2.2 each. The pipeline favours freight and harbours: the Transnet upgrade of Saldanha port, the completed R693 million Malmesbury bypass, harbour redevelopment at Lambert's Bay, Elands Bay and Laaiplek and rural broadband. No capital is committed to accommodation or payments infrastructure and no airport is planned. The municipality adds that products, guesthouses and new hubs are emerging without an organised development strategy.[^175]
rewrites.41FC93C0: No scheduled visitor transport links the coastal towns. The N2 and R43 carry access, the Cape Town to Caledon rail line is freight only and no public tourism transport connects Hermanus, Stanford, Elim or Agulhas. The district reports that limited reliable transport holds back solo travellers, while seasonal City Sightseeing services have raised traffic. The pipeline is small: the R81.7 million Agulhas lighthouse precinct, a R17 million re-gravelling of the Malgas road and Whale Coast route packaging. It gives the route an eastern anchor but leaves the De Hoop corridor without accommodation investment. It funds neither online booking nor products for the months outside whale season.[^177]
rewrites.2BFE0128: The Central Karoo is a corridor that visitors cross, not yet a destination they choose. It is the province's smallest tourism base. Occupancy follows N1 transit traffic and not destination demand. About 220,000 visitors a year go to its participating attractions. It was the only district where visitor numbers grew, by 3.3%, over a period the source does not state. Beaufort West and the Karoo National Park form the core, while Prince Albert and the Swartberg Pass hold the only boutique leisure stock. Commercial and leisure attractions are near-absent, with a category score of 1.2. The niche assets are real: dark skies, the Southern African Large Telescope, fossil trails and Matjiesfontein.[^178]
rewrites.724FB71B: Access rests on one road. The N1 is the only reliable corridor. The district has no scheduled air service, no tourism shuttle and no public transport. Beyond the N1, fuel, retail, healthcare and connectivity thin out, summer heat shortens the visiting season and truck congestion threatens the transit trade that sustains operators. Tourism offices are under-resourced and destination marketing is close to nil. The Infrastructure Report gives no pipeline for the district: its only slide in that position covers Route 62 and the Klein Karoo. No committed project can therefore be named for the Central Karoo itself.[^179]
rewrites.7F79097C: Six touring routes carry visitors between those districts and one is rated ready for international visitors (Table 2.18). The Infrastructure Report rates each Ready, Developing or Gap on access, accommodation, safety and bookability. The Garden Route carries the same four ratings as the Cape Peninsula yet is rated Developing.[^180]
rewrites.22973F40: Only the Cape Peninsula route is rated Ready and the longer outer routes fall short on access, accommodation or bookability.
rewrites.7DF3A519: Source: Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026: route cards p29, p39, p50, p61, p72, p83; scorecards p30, p40, p51, p62, p73, p84. Distances are approximate; dimensions not listed are rated Ready. Two route cards are mislabelled in the deck and each route is shown with its own figures. Emerging is not a defined rating (Appendix A4). Main gap is this report's reading.
rewrites.19AD5CB1: Services hold up better than access. Accommodation scores 3.3 or more for attractiveness in every district, so quality is not the main divide. Access is: strong product sits where visitors cannot easily reach it and infrastructure falls away fastest with distance from Cape Town. Dispersal therefore needs deliberate corridor investment and will not follow from spillover (Table 2.19).[^185]
rewrites.4F246B77: Each district has a distinct strength and a distinct asset; outside the Metro the weakness is access or service depth.
rewrites.66CF11B2: Attractions cluster along three corridors and variety falls off beyond them. The Cape corridor holds the most varied base in a compact area, while the Cape Winelands corridor centres narrowly on vineyards and scenery. The N2 corridor delivers outdoor and adventure products, most without interpretation or heritage content. The Overberg and the West Coast hold marine and wildflower assets that the Infrastructure Report finds largely inactive, with no guided tours, interpretation centres or bookable product around them. The Central Karoo and the northern interior have no anchor product.[^186]
rewrites.2277FB99: Accommodation concentrates in the same three corridors. The Cape corridor has the widest range, skewed to four-star and five-star properties. The Cape Winelands form a premium cluster with no budget tier. The Garden Route is lined with self-catering units and resorts and is short of the quality-graded hotels that anchor midweek, conference and business travel. Supply thins across the inland Overberg, West Coast and Central Karoo, which leaves no chain of stock for multi-night touring. Two of the report's province-wide claims on accommodation are qualified below.[^187]
rewrites.1A0FBA7F: Dining and retail narrow fastest outside the core. Most tourism-oriented eateries sit along the Metro's coastal belt, in the Cape Winelands and on the Garden Route's N2 corridor, with Hermanus, Langebaan, Paternoster, Swellendam and Prince Albert as regional dining nodes. Elsewhere large inland areas offer little beyond franchise fast food. Township food economies remain outside mainstream itineraries.[^188]
rewrites.77FAE7A9: Beyond the Metro the visitor drives. Airports, rail and charging points cluster around Cape Town and the Garden Route. Car rental concentrates in the main towns and airports. The Infrastructure Report finds the N2 to be the only continuous tourism corridor between regions and so a single point of failure. Large parts of the province outside the Metro and the Garden Route remain effectively car-only. That narrows the market to visitors willing to drive, the fourth barrier to conversion (section 2.1).[^189]
rewrites.62406B15: Passenger rail has collapsed as a mode. Trainsets fell from about 110 in 1995 to about 91, pushing some 400,000 commuters onto saturated roads. Congestion in the Metro costs an estimated R2.8 billion a year. Metrorail still runs 460 km, five lines and 104 of 121 stations, with 22.7 million passenger trips in FY2025. No line reaches the airport, the network is rated functionally unusable for tourism and the MyCiTi bus service to the airport remains suspended.[^190]
rewrites.40F681B6: The Southern Line is the nearest thing to a rail product for visitors. It strings together Muizenberg, Kalk Bay and Simon's Town as a low-cost scenic corridor. The Infrastructure Report describes it as fully operational with hop-on day passes. This report does not carry that description: trains run to Fish Hoek and regular service on the Simon's Town section is unconfirmed (section 2.5). The line's visitor branding dates to 2007. Beyond the Metro rail tourism rests on private heritage operators.[^191]
rewrites.329D97F2: Roads carry almost every visitor movement and public transport rarely offers an alternative. The Department of Mobility reports that limited reliable public transport constrains visitor mobility across the province. It is assessing a rapid rail link between Cape Town and George. Overland touring meets its own constraints. C-BRTA reports that tour operators avoid some Mozambique border routes because of terrain, distance and road safety. It also reports that taxi operators extort cross-border tours at border posts.[^192]
rewrites.5C58F47F: Utilities limit what remote and fast-growing nodes can host. The Diagnostic found in December 2025 that water scarcity caps visitor load in high-growth nodes such as the Garden Route. It also found that load shedding raised costs and degraded the experience in peripheral districts. Power has since steadied: Eskom reported 539 days without load shedding in November 2026, though GreenCape finds that grid-connection constraints remain. The airport has no fuel pipeline and depends on road tankers. The 2017 to 2018 water crisis left a lasting perception of resource pressure.[^193]
rewrites.5BA88D3E: The remedies are named but not scheduled. Four transport enablers are listed, none dated or costed: the Cape Town Integrator, rail restoration and devolution, a high-speed city to airport link and George to Cape Winelands passenger rail. PRASA's R21.1 billion programme and the City's R123 billion, 30-year devolution case cover fleet and lines. Neither carries a tourism product or an airport link.[^195]
rewrites.4FBAFE1B: Beds are short in particular places and no bed count yet sizes the gap. The profiles name the places: mid-market stock in the Cape Winelands, hotels and graded inland stock on the West Coast and the country east of Hermanus. On the West Coast overnight stays remain below the provincial average. The Infrastructure Report goes further and maps no mid-scale branded product anywhere between luxury estates and basic self-catering, a claim this report does not carry across the province.[^196]
rewrites.76A9F867: Sizing that gap takes more than a bed count. A usable supply comparison weighs rooms, bed types, trading periods, price points, meeting space, accessibility and committed developments against validated demand. A full hotel on peak weekends signals compression, not a year-round shortage. Branded stock also exists outside the Metro: George has the Protea Hotel by Marriott George King George, with 109 rooms and four event rooms, the largest seating 300. The question is which configuration, price point, location or capacity is missing and where.
rewrites.50E33085: Regional accommodation is listed online, which qualifies a second claim: that most rural properties are absent from online travel agencies. A desk test on 10 November 2026 found a property-specific platform listing for all 13 accommodation cases outside the operational core and all eight core comparators. The cases were chosen, not sampled. They favour established businesses, so the result gives counterexamples and not a provincial rate. Experiences differ. Of eight named attractions outside the core, three appeared on an experience marketplace, each as a stop on a tour. Guides and community product often sell only by phone.[^197]
rewrites.2AFAC83C: Prominence, inventory and sales are the open questions. No test has yet ranked regional product in a traveller's search, checked rooms on common dates or traced a sale. One major platform discloses that commission and programme participation can influence ranking. The Competition Commission examined sponsored ranking in 2023. A listing can therefore exist and still earn little exposure or earn it at a cost to the operator.
rewrites.343B1C2E: Online booking is one part of the sixth barrier to conversion, difficulty finding information (section 2.1). The evidence does not show it to be the main limit on regional growth. Where rooms are listed, the next gain is quality that shows on the booking platforms, as in Valencia (section 2.2).
rewrites.6EEB8469: Short-term rentals are a large and largely uncounted layer of the province's accommodation supply. A March 2026 snapshot of one platform's listings counted 26,991 in Cape Town, 1,953 in Overstrand, 1,413 in Knysna, 1,404 in Stellenbosch and 1,226 in Bitou; no comparable count was found for George. A listing is not a bed available tonight and a municipal count cannot stand for its towns.
rewrites.24CF37D4: Cape Town's stock is concentrated and commercial in structure. Of 27,760 listings in September 2026, 23,458 were entire homes or flats and 62.5% sat with hosts listing more than one property, though a manager is not necessarily an owner. Three wards (115, 54 and 77) held 43.8% of listings. Some 18,199 listings carried a review in the past year, a proxy for activity rather than occupancy. Their advertised capacity of 103,550 guests is not a count of available peak beds.
rewrites.4FCCD7BD: Three wards hold 43.8% of Cape Town's advertised listings and most listings in every ward shown are entire homes.
rewrites.6B44DFD3: The rules are municipal and in motion. Cape Town's 2026/27 tariff rates commercial property at 2.41 times the residential rate. Its Rates Policy treats a home let short for more than half its annual room nights as commercial for rating. That threshold sets a rate, not a limit on letting. The City consulted from August to October 2026 on registration and platform data sharing, with category changes anticipated from July 2027. Nationally, a draft code was published in March 2026. The Minister of Tourism has stated that the current Act does not empower her to regulate the sector.
rewrites.5027CDAA: Air access drew the fewest supply insights and that reflects who was heard. One summarised insight covers it, on limited air access and long ground transfers from Cape Town International. No stakeholder named the airport's capacity as a constraint and no airline or airport was among the 16 organisations. The runway's absence from stakeholder concerns is therefore a gap in the record, not a finding. Later engagement phases are planned, not held. The runway itself is a national lever, held by ACSA (section 2.5).[^202]
rewrites.7D245B1D: Supply paces growth at the peak and beyond the Metro; it does not cap growth across the year. Cape Town International is the gateway risk, because the runway limits the peak hours and relief arrives on ACSA's dates in the early 2030s. Outside the peak hours and months seats remain, on the hub routes above all. Conversion work and seat retention therefore move first and route cases follow as runway capacity arrives.[^203]
rewrites.232DE45C: Beyond the Metro the province has the assets and the task is to turn them into complete, accessible visits. The Garden Route, the Cape Winelands and the Overberg have product and need transport between towns, packaging and service depth to lengthen stays. The West Coast and the Central Karoo show that distinct assets are not enough where services, mobility and year-round demand stay weak. Transport is a problem of connection and dispersal, not a province-wide shortage of capacity.[^204]
rewrites.034BB7E0: **Objective 7, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes.** Eleven routes run above 80% and fares are likely to rise before seats. Seats pace growth at the peak: the runway limits peak hours until relief arrives on ACSA's dates, about 2033 on the planning timeline. The 2026 Gulf disruption showed that hubs in one region share risk. Seat retention and frequencies on full routes come first and new route cases follow as runway capacity arrives.
rewrites.71B9F93D: **Objective 9, Accelerate tourism-enabling internal mobility.** Accessibility falls from 4.7 to 1.0 and public transport is absent beyond the Metro, which leaves most of the province to visitors willing to drive. Stakeholders filed 18 insights on mobility, ten of them rated High. The Department of Mobility's draft Tourism Transport Strategy already plans the airport link and tourist route signage (section 2.5). The MyCiTi airport service is suspended and the grant behind MyCiTi ends in 2027/28.
rewrites.069B9FCF: **Objective 10, Support diversified route and product development; objective 11, Align visitor experience in-destination.** One of six touring routes rates Ready and every district outside the Metro is outpaced by its own assets. The gaps differ by place: transfers in the Cape Winelands, depth east of Hermanus, beds and year-round product on the West Coast and services along Route 62. The mid-market gap is a product question to test place by place. Nine of the ten places international tourists visit most are in the Metro.
rewrites.54983DBF: **Objectives 2, 4, 5 and 6, from the air side.** Winter seats fall to 6.4% of the year in June, so the green season has room that the peak lacks. No seat flies direct to Asia today and the hub routes still have seats, so conversion runs through the hubs. The mature long-haul routes are the fullest. Routes to five regional markets run above 80% and are named for more capacity.
rewrites.7208A055: Alignment across those tiers is thin. Stakeholders described strain at SA Tourism and a lack of fiscal space. More than twenty bodies produce tourism data, yet the Diagnostic finds no single view of visitor behaviour, which leaves strategy reacting rather than predicting. The Department of Mobility reports the same split in its own field: mobility responsibilities are spread across the three tiers and local governments often lack the capacity and funding to carry them out.[^207]
rewrites.317902CA: Stakeholders said more about the enabling goal than about either of the others. Of the 223 insights in the engagement record, 91 are coded to this goal: 48 rated High, 38 Medium and 5 Low. Each of the 16 organisations contributed at least one. Stats SA and the national Department of Tourism spoke to this goal alone. The record's summary condenses the goal into 17 statements under six themes, without ratings. Ratings sit on the organisation rows only and are not defined (Table 2.21).[^208]
rewrites.34726594: Policy and data sharing and collaboration reach the most organisations; institutional arrangements carry the largest share of High ratings.
rewrites.4C35C6DD: Entry rules are changing as this report is written. The Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) launched officially on 12 August 2026, after pilot access for China, India, Indonesia and Mexico. By early November 2026 it was reported as open to 53 nationalities, with the eVisa platform to close on 1 December 2026; this comes from trade reporting, partly corroborated by an embassy notice. A R500 electronic processing fee has applied since 17 August 2026 and a separate R425 visa fee applies where payable. The Trusted Tour Operator Scheme (TTOS) had issued 49,725 visas by 22 January 2026, an approval rate of about 95%, with 45 operators added in August 2025 to the original 65. A visa issued is not an arrival, so the test is authorisations matched to arrivals.
rewrites.738740A5: African entry rules vary by passport, not by region. Ordinary passport holders from Ghana and Kenya have 90 days a year. Botswana and Zimbabwe are in the 90-day category, while Namibia, Zambia and Tanzania carry annual qualifications. Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritius and Mozambique are in the 30-day category. Angola permits visits of up to 30 days within a 90-day annual allowance. Nigeria is not ordinarily exempt and SADC membership confers no uniform waiver. No comparable processing-time series exists for visa-required African markets.
rewrites.5E6C9B8D: National Treasury issued MFMA Circular No. 131 on 31 March 2025. It distinguishes an unrequited transfer under section 67 of the Municipal Finance Management Act from a purchase of services, which must follow constitutional procurement and municipal supply-chain rules. In practice it interrupted established municipal funding of LTOs, as the Department of Economic Development finds. Garden Route officials reported in March 2026 that Calitzdorp and Ladismith could not operate fully, that Calitzdorp's office closed from November to February and that Oudtshoorn, De Rust and Plettenberg Bay were affected. The circular does not prohibit funding tourism organisations: the contracted-services route remains open and the City of Cape Town processed its first Cape Town Tourism payment that way (City mid-year report, January 2026). The scale is not known: no source counts the organisations affected or their funding before and after, George's integrated tourism unit was unaffected and the Garden Route reports are attributed statements, not an audited inventory.[^216]
rewrites.7CBB358C: Procurement discipline predates the circular and partnerships lapse as well as grants. An earlier Auditor-General finding at Mossel Bay recorded tourism spend as irregular where procurement was not followed. Mossel Bay's tourism body still rates its public-private model a structural advantage because it decides faster than a fully municipal one. FEDHASA reports that the memorandum behind the Discover Garden Route partnership has expired and that municipal control over operating terms limited its flexibility.[^217]
rewrites.6491D0D2: Mandates blur at district level. The West Coast District Municipality reports a mandate disconnect between the district, local municipalities and LTOs that leaves tourism development without a clear home. The district moved from a tourism development unit to destination marketing roles. LTO contracts and budgets are weighted the same way. It asks for tourism development to be written into integrated development plans and spatial frameworks, with reporting.[^218]
rewrites.07986C15: Fiscal pressure is turning attention to a tourism levy and blended finance. The Department of Economic Development reports that tight fiscal space is prompting consideration of a levy. The Department of Mobility sees a need for climate, development, blended-finance and private-sector models. Its draft transport framework plans its own business case for a tourist levy to fund tourism transport. CapeNature reports that it cannot rely on public funding alone and now runs tourism as a revenue-earning business.[^219]
rewrites.47327A36: Capital is tightest where the plan needs new sellers. SATVITO reports that access to funding remains a persistent constraint for township and village tourism businesses and that limited information on support programmes keeps them from help that exists. The committed capital in section 2.4 builds airports, ports, roads, transit and precincts, but none of it funds the bodies that manage and sell the destination. The plan cannot rest on LTOs until their services are contracted on a lawful route and their mandates are settled.[^220]
rewrites.5DE44DCC: Sustainable growth starts with what the destination can carry. Water scarcity limits visitor load in high-growth nodes such as the Garden Route. Boulders is near carrying capacity and no source yet measures the carrying capacity of any flagship (section 2.4). Climate adds a dated cost. Robben Island Museum loses about R16 million a year to weather-cancelled trips. CapeNature reports climate-related flooding, fire and heat closing sites. CapeNature also finds off-grid solar and self-sufficiency increasingly necessary to keep remote sites in service. Sustainable destination management is risk management for the province's flagship product today and should be funded as such, not as a later add-on.[^221]
rewrites.7F071531: Structures for the first task exist. The province has a climate response forum, an implementation plan dated March 2023 and support for municipalities. Its Water Resilience Strategy runs from 2025 to 2035. DEDAT offers tourism disaster-risk guidance and one-day training. Wesgro's Water Communications Centre of 2017/18 is a local precedent for joint crisis messaging. The Green Tourism Incentive Programme is closed pending review.
rewrites.245FDBF6: Capacity is tighter than supply plans suggest. The City's August 2026 position is stable supply with rising restriction risk. The first Faure water arrives only in 2031 (section 2.4). George's and Knysna's capacity figures depend on assets operating. Blue Drop and Green Drop results do not certify spare capacity for a hotel. Floods in May 2026 damaged CapeNature roads, trails and buildings; by June, 85% of its reserves reported some damage.
rewrites.24B60728: Collaboration and data sharing are the concerns stakeholders share most widely and they differ in tone. On collaboration, Medium ratings outnumber High and many insights describe platforms that work. On data sharing, High ratings outnumber Medium and most insights describe a gap (Table 2.21).[^222]
rewrites.6004A39B: The data holders describe what the public series can show. Stats SA publishes monthly international tourism data with a lag of about one month, covering traveller volumes, trip purpose, mode of transport and regional distribution. Its domestic tourism survey draws on a large household sample. Stats SA is raising its household sample from 30,000 to 40,000 while it tests a continuous population survey. It is also developing safety and security data for analysis at municipal level.[^223]
rewrites.2D055E7B: Coordination is hard everywhere, as the comparators show (section 2.2). Yet the platforms for collaboration already exist here. FEDHASA points to the Joint Association Members Meeting Sessions (JAMMS). Through it Cape Town Tourism, FEDHASA Cape, SAACI Western Cape and SATSA Western Cape coordinate with Wesgro, the Western Cape Government and the City of Cape Town. Stats SA compiles the tourism national accounts through a cross-agency task team with SA Tourism and government departments. C-BRTA runs tour-operator forums twice a year. What is missing is an agreed way to share data across those bodies, not another forum.[^226]
rewrites.62A2F41F: The forums serve marketing better than development. The West Coast District Municipality reports that provincial and regional forums are dominated by destination marketing and that provincial support, Wesgro's strategy and district needs are poorly matched on grants, capacity building and skills. Where the task is selling, collaboration is reported to work: the CTICC describes effective joint bidding and !Khwa ttu markets itself through LTOs, community partners and content creators.[^227]
rewrites.4195F5A5: Policy settings lag the task in several places. The Department of Economic Development reports a provincial policy gap: legislation is limited and earlier policy and master-planning frameworks are out of date. At !Khwa ttu, transport cost keeps public schools away. Curriculum-linked visits at scale would need support from the Education Department or another public mechanism. Circular 131 is a further case (see Funding and mandates above).[^228]
rewrites.09C85381: Two plans reach into the visitor's trip. The Department of Mobility's draft Provincial Land Transport Framework includes a Tourism Transport Strategy, which plans to revive the MyCiTi airport service with ACSA and to sign and maintain tourist routes. The City's framework for 2019 to 2024 set out a Tourist Safety Programme of secure zones in higher-risk tourism areas, a Tourist Police unit, victim support and safety forums. Parts of it now run. The action plan should build on both rather than start new ones. Which parts of the department's Tourism Transport Strategy are adopted, funded or running is not confirmed.[^229]
rewrites.6F583C24: Mobility evidence is thin and its funding is at risk. No verified visitor mode split exists: Wesgro's Cape Winelands survey for January to June 2025 records rental cars for 29.29% of international respondents, with 85.35% of domestic transport answers missing. The City says MyCiTi's Public Transport Network Grant ends in 2027/28, with R7.1 billion committed to the Cape Flats expansion and 23 million annual trips. It says that fleet and services are at risk. Phase 2A is therefore a funded-delivery milestone, not a given. The MyCiTi airport service is suspended and ACSA's own pages conflict on where e-hailing pickup sits.
rewrites.7467392F: Rail and regional buses are closer to use than to a visitor product. The Southern Line runs from Cape Town to Fish Hoek, with a Simon's Town section whose regular service PRASA has yet to confirm. Trains do not normally run on Sundays or public holidays. Boulders needs a transfer from Simon's Town station. The City's rail business plan favours transferred services with private operating participation. The National Rail Master Plan went to consultation in April 2026; neither is an executed devolution.
rewrites.3828E0E6: GO GEORGE requires its own R45 smart card, which can be loaded with cash, a debit or credit card or a SASSA card. Its single fare from July 2026 is R18.50. What is unresolved is tapping a bank card directly on the bus, which national integrated-fare regulations already contemplate. GO GEORGE trialled an airport service in September 2026.
rewrites.4C7921A2: Activity figures are not crime rates. The City records 2,895 motorist assists by N2 patrols from September 2024 to January 2026 (1,061 of them camera-detected) and 80% of highway incidents since July 2025 were answered within five minutes. SANParks appointed a visitor-safety manager for Table Mountain in December 2025, yet a robbery on Lion's Head in October 2026 prompted a public dispute over patrol coverage. Tourism Monitors figures count people trained, not people placed. SAPS retains command and the Western Cape Government holds oversight under section 206 of the Constitution.
rewrites.4B15A45D: The province has a starting figure. If the 300,000 ambition uses the same definition, it sits about 17% above the 2023 level. That reading is conditional on the definition, which the workstream confirms with the department in 2027.[^232]
rewrites.1F55DD0C: The same work is needed at community scale. Community profiles do not count tourism employment inside their boundaries. The figures are node-side instead, such as about 4,700 formal Town Centre jobs for 82,393 employed Mitchells Plain residents. Need rests on fifteen-year-old Census data. CapeNature, the West Coast District and the Overberg raise skills gaps that the labour analysis can size.[^233]
rewrites.76BB5CBD: Skills evidence has the same limits. CATHSSETA's 2026/27 discretionary grants offer a funding route, not a vacancy count. Industry employment totals cannot identify unfilled posts. DEDAT's plan records pressure on guide registration, with application growth, overtime and burnout. It commits to workflow fixes. National Mandarin training of about 30 guides in early 2026 is not 30 additional Western Cape guides.
rewrites.6450DB28: Note: Resident shares from Census 2011. R259m and R547m are reference points, not adopted targets. The R4m to R10m bar is drawn at R10m and the 0.02% to 0.04% share is too small to draw to scale. SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p5.
rewrites.79BD73A9: Organisation is the binding constraint in 11 of the 20. Ten have no identified active tourism body and nine show no benefit visible to residents.[^238]
rewrites.121AF459: Stakeholders describe the same gap from the seller's side. SATVITO reports that many township and village businesses lack market readiness (from compliance to an understanding of buyers) and so cannot reach trade platforms or incentive programmes. The Overberg District finds that established capital has driven tourism development and that community products need sustained mentoring. The West Coast District Municipality reports no medium-term approach behind township tourism. Three of these four insights are rated High.[^240]
rewrites.1380FE11: After a seller, safety is the next gate a visit must pass. Nine of the 20 communities record a safety-perception gap and five record extortion. Seven stakeholder organisations raised safety. SATVITO reports that negative perceptions of the townships constrain demand for their product. Section 2.1 treats safety perceptions as a barrier to conversion; the concern here is the visit itself. Tourism activity alone cannot resolve crime or extortion. Safety is therefore a launch requirement in its own right, not an outcome of the pilot. No community pilot should open until it is met.[^241]
rewrites.42C59319: The largest group of long-listed communities sits near a node and has something worth visiting. Each type needs its own first move. Near a node with assets underused, 49 long-listed and 11 shortlisted communities need sellers organised and a slot in the node's itineraries, procurement and events. Near a node with nothing inside, 43 long-listed and 6 shortlisted communities need a seller first, then one anchor asset under a covenant, then integration.[^242]
rewrites.16ED1F81: **Objective 14, Embed sustainable tourism and manage climate risk; objective 15, Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies.** Water and site capacity are under pressure, floods have damaged the reserves and weather cancellations cost revenue. Tourism funding sits below peer destinations and capital is tightest for township and village businesses. The Department of Mobility proposes its own tourist levy case.
rewrites.21DE4BDE: **Objective 10, Support diversified route and product development; objective 15.** Assets follow sellers and route products, not the reverse.
rewrites.77D2D46A: **Objective 19, Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits.** Wesgro works by escalation backed with evidence, because visas and air rights sit nationally.
